questions.question: What quantity appears on the left side of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality?
options: The determinant of a matrix of coordinates.
The angle itself in radians.
The sum of the vector coordinates.
The absolute value of the inner product.

questions.question: What does Cauchy-Schwarz say the inner product cannot exceed in absolute value?
options: The dimension of the vector space.
The sum of the two vector lengths.
The larger of the two first coordinates.
The product of the two vector lengths.

questions.question: What happens to the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality when two vectors are orthogonal?
options: The left side is $0$.
The inequality is no longer valid.
The product of the norms becomes negative.
The right side must be $0$ for nonzero vectors.

questions.question: Why does Cauchy-Schwarz help define the angle between nonzero vectors?
options: It makes the dot product always positive.
It avoids using norms.
It guarantees $(x\cdot y)/(\|x\|\|y\|)$ lies between $-1$ and $1$.
It makes every angle equal to $90^\circ$.

questions.question: When does equality hold in Cauchy-Schwarz for nonzero real vectors?
options: When the vectors are orthogonal.
When the vectors have the same first coordinate.
When the vectors have different dimensions.
When the vectors are scalar multiples of each other.

questions.question: For $x=(1,0)$ and $y=(0,1)$, what is $|x\cdot y|$?
options: $\sqrt2$

questions.question: For $x=(3,4)$ and $y=(1,0)$, what is $|x\cdot y|$?
Which inequality instance is correct for $x=(1,2)$ and $y=(2,1)$?
options: $4\leq\sqrt5$

questions.question: If $x=y\neq0$, what is $|x\cdot y|$ compared with $\|x\|\|y\|$?
options: The comparison is undefined.
The right side is always zero.
They are equal.
The left side is always smaller.

questions.question: Why is the absolute value necessary in $|x\cdot y|\leq\|x\|\|y\|$?
options: The inequality is only about positive coordinates, universally and without exception.
Norms can be negative.
The inner product can be negative when vectors point in largely opposite directions.
The dot product is never real.

questions.question: What would Cauchy-Schwarz rule out for two unit vectors?
options: A dot product equal to $1.4$.
A dot product equal to $-1$.
A dot product equal to $0$.
A dot product equal to $1$.

questions.question: Why is Cauchy-Schwarz stronger than just saying $x\cdot y\leq\|x\|\|y\|$?
options: It removes the need for inner products.
It also controls large negative inner products.
It applies only when $x=y$.
It gives equality for every pair of vectors.

questions.question: If $\|x\|=2$ and $\|y\|=3$, what is the largest possible value of $|x\cdot y|$?
If $u$ and $v$ are unit vectors, which value cannot be $u\cdot v$?
For $x=(2,1)$ and $y=(1,2)$, compute both sides of Cauchy-Schwarz.
options: $|x\cdot y|=4$ and $\|x\|\|y\|=\sqrt5$

questions.question: Why does equality in Cauchy-Schwarz signal that two nonzero vectors lie on the same line through the origin?
options: Equality forces both vectors to have norm zero.
Equality occurs exactly when one vector is a scalar multiple of the other.
Equality can occur only in one-dimensional spaces.
Equality occurs exactly when the vectors are orthogonal, irrespective of the particular case.

questions.question: Expanding $\|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+2(x\cdot y)+\|y\|^2$, which theorem bounds the cross term to yield the triangle inequality?
options: The triangle inequality is used to define the dot product.
They are unrelated because one uses sums and the other uses products.
Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the cross term when expanding $\|x+y\|^2$.
Cauchy-Schwarz replaces vector addition by determinant expansion.

questions.question: Let $x=(1,2,2)$ and $y=(2,0,1)$. Which Cauchy-Schwarz comparison is correct?
options: $3\sqrt5\leq4$
$4\leq3\sqrt5$
$4\leq\sqrt5$

questions.question: If $\|x\|=4$ and $\|y\|=5$, which value of $x\cdot y$ is impossible?
